annotations.text: Reference: the settled visual decision and card design.
Final landing page: desktop and mobile, dark and light.

Every desktop app screen from here down is a fixed 1440x900, a real 16:10 viewport, not sized to whatever content happened to be on it. Content that doesn't fit scrolls inside the screen on its own custom-styled scrollbar (never the default browser one), the shell around it stays put. Landing pages, mobile artboards, and the small floating overlay components (turn banner, away widget, chat panel, the import progress callout) are the exceptions, they're a different medium or deliberately compact by design.

Auth screens, in progress, desktop only. Log in and Create account are one screen with a toggle switcher at the top, not two separate pages: the two Login/Register artboards show the same screen in its two toggle states. Forgot password is its own standalone screen. OAuth2 redirect is the transient handoff screen while that flow completes, no real content of its own, shown for completeness.

Playlists and content, desktop only. Your playlists (personal library), Explore public playlists (story 30's published-playlist capability), Playlist detail, Song detail in both its states (verified/report-only, and needs-review/report-plus-confirm), Edit song details (manual-entry only), Add songs, Edit playlist, and Join by invite. All reuse the same left sidebar; song playback always links out to the real YouTube page or app, never an embedded player. Only the dark theme is being iterated on right now, light versions get ported once each page settles, so several pages currently only have a dark artboard. Terminology: "Join" is for accepting an invite link and becoming a real member of a playlist (Join by invite); "Save" (Explore public playlists) is for adding someone else's public playlist to your own library without becoming a member of it. Playlist detail offers two ways to add content: "Add song" and "Import playlist", both fully designed as their own flows below, plus story 45's third path, copying songs straight from another accessible playlist, folded into the Import playlist flow.

Editing is reserved for the tier that actually needs it. Verified data already went through source agreement or an admin's manual review, and needs-review data came from real (if disagreeing) source reconciliation, hand-editing either one back out undermines the trust the pipeline just established. Only manual-entry songs, no source had any data at all, are directly editable: their row gets a red badge and a pencil icon on Playlist detail, routing to Edit song details. Needs-review rows keep an amber badge and the usual eye icon, routing to Song detail, read-only, but with a confirm ("is this correct?") action added alongside report, both shown on the needs-review variant below. The "Review now" link on the summary banner jumps straight to the first flagged row in the list.

Add songs is two paths. The main page (search and queue) lets you search the existing song database, add several at once, and see everything queued before confirming; both the results list and the queue panel scroll on their own custom-styled scrollbar and now extend to match each other's height. "Add a new song" is a separate 3-step flow shown as its own artboards: 1) paste a YouTube link, 2) metadata is fetched automatically (no dedicated screen needed, it's instant), 3) review. Fields are locked when the AI is confident (with a "Report and edit manually" override for when it's confidently wrong), or left as empty, editable fields with placeholder text when it isn't sure. It never fabricates a partial guess.

Import playlist, the second way to add content from Playlist detail, now with two sources. Choosing "From YouTube" leads to the same crawl flow as before: step 1 takes a playlist link, step 2 lists every song and crawls them one at a time, each row starting with the raw YouTube data (video title and channel name, muted and in italics) and a spinning fetch indicator, then updating in place to the real title, artist, and release year with a checkmark once processed. Choosing "From an existing playlist" is instant instead: pick a playlist you've joined or found public, and every song copies over immediately, no fetching, since it's already in the database. Either way, closing the import screen doesn't cancel it: a temporary icon appears in the left sidebar below Group lobby while an import is active, and a small toast shows the progress once, then fades after a few seconds. Both reopen the import screen. That whole pattern is shown isolated in its own board below.

Gameplay, desktop only. A session has no fixed round count, it ends whenever the first player reaches the group's configured win-condition card count. Group lobby drops the card/panel look entirely: the join code sits centered and large with a copy-link action under it, members scatter around it at varied distances and angles, each tilted slightly, with a slow, subtle drift animation, not literal movement or a symmetric grid. Avatar size is dynamic, not fixed: 112px at 2 players, 108px at 4, 102px at 8, all three deliberately close together rather than shrinking hard as the count climbs. Distance from the code is generous at every count, clear of the join-code label and the copy-link action around it, not just the big digits themselves. Two more artboards show the same layout at 2 and at 8 players, since how it holds up at the group-size extremes matters more than the 4-player middle case alone. The bottom bar holds four labeled buttons, start game, chat, and settings grouped together, leave lobby set apart on the right; two further artboards show settings and chat each open as their own popup, both undimmed and anchored near the button that opens them rather than a centered dialog, chat reusing the same message-list pattern as the standalone Text chat overlay artboard and the semi-transparent bottom-left placement GAME_DESIGN.md specs. The voice sidebar shows the not-yet-joined state: existing participants listed with no mute/deafen/leave controls of your own, a dashed join-call circle trailing the list. Then the game session in its two views. Player is shown across six artboards walking the full turn: an unplaced card rendered as a large animated version of the app's equalizer mark, dragging it onto the timeline with neighboring cards fanning open and wobbling until the drop lands, the card settled face down once locked in with playback stopped, a countdown before betting opens, the betting window itself with the first token staked and everyone else locked out, exactly one bet accepted per round staking the bettor's own guessed placement rather than a correct or incorrect vote, and the reveal once the round closes. The artist/title guess box stays available across every one of those states, since guessing isn't tied to whose turn it is to place a card. DJ (song playback, always a link-out to the real YouTube page or app with the audio-sharing warning attached, plus the actual round-flow controls: pause, play, close, end turn, reveal gated until betting closes). Results/leaderboard shows the card-count ranking alongside the two session-long guess leaderboards once the game has ended.

Overlay components used during a session: the turn notification banner, the "playing while away" floating widget, and the text chat panel. Shown isolated at natural size, not placed on a specific background.

Admin views, desktop only, dark. Gated on the ADMIN role (story 40). Catalog backlog: pending/processed/quota stats plus the bulk-enqueue form, the batch YouTube-ID filtering step happens silently, only the result is shown. Report review queue: every reportable card ranked by the five-tier priority order, with the actual signals behind each rank (report count, convergence, confirmations) rather than one opaque score, and a manual resolve action, nothing here auto-applies a suggested year.
